A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-stage steering work, renamed from RAS to MoRAS. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety, utility, throughput, ablation and qualitative results in Section 4 and Appendices C-H.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds attack, calibration, over-refusal and computational-cost results in Section 4 and the supplementary material.

M1.justification: The core EWRE and adaptive-steering equations remain unchanged. A limited input change is documented: v1 Appendix A.1 includes the original question when generating visual context, whereas v3 Supplementary Section 1.1 and Algorithm 1 use the image and context-generation prompt alone. Renaming RAS to MoRAS is not itself a method change.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original safety and utility benchmarks while adding JOOD attacks using out-of-distribution image combinations, gradient-based visual adversarial attacks, XSTest and OR-Bench over-refusal tasks, and suffix-injected MM-Safety queries. These substantially broaden the evaluated input conditions and safety requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds AutoSteer and ASTRA to the retained FigStep, CoCA, ECSO and ETA comparisons, including safety, utility and throughput evaluations. This introduces direct comparisons with contemporary multimodal steering defenses, beyond v1's prompting and response-refinement baselines.

E3.justification: Default risk calibration changes from 100 unsafe SPA-VL examples to 100 held-out examples from AutoSteer's calibration dataset, with revised parameters. v3 also adds LLaVA-OneVision-7B, calibration wall-clock measurements, and a visual-adversarial protocol averaging four perturbation settings over 200 prompts. New baseline tuning experiments use GPT-4o for MM-Vet scoring; the main benchmark evaluation retains GPT-4-0613.

E4.justification: v3 adds calibration-source/size sensitivity, alternative-object FDR analysis, fixed-strength steering comparisons, suffix robustness, baseline hyperparameter sweeps and overhead breakdowns. Prototype-source and refusal-vector studies are revised and expanded in some respects, although the prototype-source study narrows to one backbone. v1's binary-steering and image-removal ASR ablations disappear; related image-removal FDR analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Added calibration sample-size comparisons and benchmark averages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new attacks, comparators, a backbone and computational costs, and replaces several retained-model scores. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, reported MM-Safety/SPA-VL/FigStep ASRs change from 4.1/8.3/2.2 to 2.6/7.6/2.8 under revised calibration, rather than establishing a controlled performance gain. Rankings are no longer uniformly favorable: v3 Table 1 reports VAA ASR of 12.1 for ETA versus 14.3 for MoRAS on this backbone.

T1.justification: The attention aggregation, FDR, prototype averaging, weighted cosine similarity, sigmoid risk mapping and refusal-vector equations retain equivalent mathematical content. The attention definition moves to supplementary material; no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central attention-based risk assessment and safety/utility claims remain, but v3 adds low calibration-data requirements and low pre-deployment cost as headline contributions. Its abstract and introduction reposition the advantage around robustness across attacks and efficiency relative to steering defenses, including a claimed 126.6-fold reduction in pre-deployment overhead.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of steering baselines' distribution-shift failures, calibration-source/size robustness, and safety versus over-refusal tradeoffs. Supplementary Section 8 replaces v1 Appendix G's attack-versus-defense explanation of refusal-vector performance with a query-specific geometric explanation. The original visual-attention mechanism remains central.

D1.justification: v3 adds executable-style pseudocode, discloses the H200 GPU and Xeon CPU used for cost measurements, details preparation procedures and timings, and specifies baseline layer, strength and threshold configurations. Calibration parameters are updated. Conversely, v1's promise to release code upon publication is removed without replacement access information.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a substantial training-alignment discussion toward direct positioning against AutoSteer and ASTRA, emphasizing calibration costs and attack generalization. New attack, over-refusal and dataset references support this expanded positioning, while several training-alignment references and discussions are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten, and RAS is renamed MoRAS. The method exposition separates the attention diagnosis from query reformulation. Lettered appendices become numbered supplementary sections with a contents guide, and implementation and sensitivity discussions are reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview diagram, restyles and reorders attention illustrations, and substantially restructures the main comparison table. LLaVA-1.5-13B results move to a supplementary table. Figure 7 gains a calibration-cost panel, while new tables and sensitivity heatmaps materially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through direct steering-defense comparisons, broader adversarial conditions, explicit over-refusal tests, and calibration sensitivity and cost breakdowns. These address important gaps in v1's evidence for robustness and practical efficiency. The gains outweigh the removed component ablations and code-release pledge. Some superiority wording exceeds Table 1's mixed rankings, and neither version quantifies run-to-run uncertainty.
